newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - Strategic road ahead for contractors.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - Strategic road ahead for contractors.

text.p: With the traditional giants of the road transport industry largely quitting the freight race, the emerging medium sized transport companies are expected to rationalise and focus more on the growing logistics sector.

While 1996/97 is expected to remain tough, brokers see an improvement in the performance of the listed smaller transport companies over the next 12-18 months with a general economic upturn, particularly in the building and retail sectors.
However, whether revenue rises convert into profit growth in a highly competitive market remains unclear, they said, amid warnings also of the impact of expected industry wage claims.

Most analysts expect to see major rationalisation in the industry over the next five years, with the field of about 12 competitors including the three key listed players - Scott Corp, Finemores and Toll Holdings.

"They will become the next tier of medium sized transport companies, what Mayne Nickless and TNT were in the 1960s and 1970s, these guys will be in the late 1990s," Justin Arter from broker J.B Were told Reuters.
"It is not a highly profitable industry but they will be pretty big," he said.

There are a number of rationalisation scenarios, led by talk of a merger of Scott Corp and Finemore, and/or the long-anticipated coming together of Scott Corp with major shareholder Alan Scott's private Scott Transport Industries.
Arter said the market was "very rugged" at the moment, due to fairly aggressive price discounting, although the three listed companies tended to operate in different niches.

Finemore had a heavy bias now in logistics for automotive companies, such as Ford and General Motors, plus an exposure to general freighting, while it was progressively divesting a lot of its cattle freighting and outback operations, he said.
Scott Corp was trying to change its focus from domestic general transport into the logistics market, with its A$40 million annual Smorgon steel contract a crucial move, he said.

Toll, which on Monday announced a rail joint venture with TNT, is seen as remaining more in general freight and has moved more quickly to grab assets from the exiting giants, buying the Interlink Distribution Services from Mayne Nickless last year and Brambles Transport Services earlier this year.
"They have a task ahead of themselves bedding that down," Arter said. "I think they will do it but they have a big task."
Scott Corp and Finemore have already delivered a good example of joint venture potential with their Smart Distribution $50 million a year contract with Australian Newsprint Mills.

Analysts believe the current takeover by Dutch postal and telecoms firm Koninklijke PTT Nederland NV (KPN) of transport giant TNT Ltd also may produce interesting opportunities for the junior transport companies.
Day Cutten analyst Nick Ross said further rationalisation and joint ventures would be demanded by the expense of the moves from express and general freight to the value added logistics.
"There are very high barriers to entry and it will require a lot of capital expenditure on their part," he told Reuters.
"As a consequence they will either have to go through joint ventures or take over their competitors," he said.

However Andrew Mullholland, of Prudential Bache Securities, warned against seeing logistics as "a magic formula" which would convert the trend to commoditisation in the transport industry to a higher barrier of entry, higher margin business.

"It is upping the entry requirements to the game, but everybody will be able to provide these ... so you are going to have to provide perhaps a one-stop shop in terms of provision of services to your customer," he said.
He said companies would have to achieve major or sole provider status with client companies while being able to pass on cost reduction benefits.
Mullholland said the industry had seen very rapid revenue growth but, as with the United States experience, that had not yet converted through to high profit growth.
"The question is: is the industry ultimately going to be able to deliver significant profit performance as well as revenue growth and I think that is a much less certain prospect," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
